what_it_does: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) is a technique for rendering photorealistic 3D scenes from photos: a neural network takes a viewpoint and a ray direction as input and predicts the color and density at every point along that ray, building up a complete image pixel by pixel. Each rendered frame requires shooting thousands of rays, and each ray requires many network evaluations, making NeRF far too slow and power-hungry for battery-powered edge devices such as phones or VR headsets. ASDR targets this with computing-in-memory (CIM) arrays — specialized hardware where arithmetic is performed directly inside the memory chip rather than moving data back and forth to a separate processor, which saves energy by cutting memory traffic. On top of that, ASDR uses adaptive sampling (dynamically firing fewer ray samples in simple regions of the scene) and data reuse (sharing computed results between neighboring rays and consecutive frames that see similar content), reducing both the number of computations and the energy cost of each computation.
